Chapter 6: Unlearning Harmful Narratives and Rewriting the Script
Have you ever caught yourself repeating a story in your head, so familiar it just slips out without a second thought? Maybe it’s that quiet inner voice whispering, “You’re too much,” or, “You’re not enough.”
These stories don’t appear out of thin air—they’re pieced together from years of little comments, media messages, and things we overhear. Most of us don’t realize how deep these narratives go, or how much they guide the choices we make, every single day.
Picture this: Someone’s scrolling through old photos. With each image, memories come flooding back—not just of places or people, but of that familiar self-critique. “I look tired.” “My arms are too big.” “Why did I wear that?” It’s such a well-rehearsed pattern, it almost feels normal. But then, out of nowhere, a new thought breaks through: “What if none of that mattered?”
That question changes everything. It’s a little unsettling, but honestly, it’s freeing.
Unlearning these harmful scripts isn’t about pretending they never existed. It’s about noticing them, pausing to ask where they came from, and deciding which ones actually deserve a place in your life. Sometimes, it means following a belief all the way back to its source—a parent’s warning, a magazine headline, or a teacher’s passing comment—and realizing, “Wait, that was never really mine.”
There’s this story I love about someone who always apologized for taking up space—at work, in relationships, even just riding the subway. One day, after getting interrupted for the third time in a meeting, they decide not to shrink back. Their voice shakes a little, but they say, “I wasn’t finished.” The room falls silent, and for a second, that old fear comes rushing in. But then... nothing bad happens. In fact, a couple of colleagues even nod in support.
That’s when it becomes clear—the script can be rewritten, one small act at a time.
Most of us don’t realize how often we police ourselves, editing what we say and do to fit someone else’s expectations. Unlearning is slow work. Sometimes it’s frustrating, but it’s always worth it. Every time an old story gets challenged, a bit more space opens up for realness and self-trust.
Over time, those old rules—the ones that used to feel set in stone—start to lose their grip. New scripts move in, ones that honor who we truly are, celebrate our differences, and make room for growth.
So, here’s the real takeaway: This journey isn’t about erasing your past. It’s about choosing which stories you want to carry with you, and gently letting the rest go.
